sections.h2: Kansas estate tax and inheritance tax
sections.html:
If the owner died after December 31, 2009, Kansas collects no estate tax. Lawmakers wrote no estate tax provisions for those deaths, so nothing is owed, and the Department of Revenue turns away returns filed for them.

That history is why outdated advice lingers. An estate tax took the place of the old inheritance tax in 1998, covering deaths on or after July 1, 1998. The version covering deaths after December 31, 2006 and before January 1, 2010 sits at K.S.A. 79-15,201 and following, and K.S.A. 79-15,253 repealed it on January 1, 2010.

For a recent death the state-level question is settled. What's left is the federal estate tax and income tax on any gain once the house is sold.

sections.h2: When the federal estate tax reaches a Kansas house
sections.html:
Only for a very large estate. A 2026 death carries a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000.

Federal figure2026 amount
Basic exclusion amount (year of death)$15,000,000
Credit equivalent at 2026 rates$5,945,800
Yearly gift exclusion, each recipient$19,000

That figure adds up everything the person owned, so a Kansas family home is usually a small slice. Under the exclusion, federal estate tax plays no role in a keep-or-sell decision.

For an heir, basis is generally what the house was worth on the day of death (IRS Publication 551). Newer guidance covers certain property whose basis must match the value finally reported for estate tax.

Timing therefore drives the income tax bill. A sale near the value at death produces a small gain, while years of appreciation enlarge it. An appraisal as of the death date is cheap insurance against a basis dispute later. The sale then falls under the rules on our Kansas capital gains page.

There is one exception. Appreciated property that you or your spouse gave the decedent within a year of death comes back to you with the decedent's adjusted basis instead.

sections.h2: Probate before selling an inherited Kansas house
sections.html:
A house titled only in the decedent's name generally can't be sold until a court names someone to act. The case is normally opened in the county where the property sits, and the executor or administrator reports to the District Court.

  • Six months: file the petition to open probate no later than 6 months after the person died.
  • Four to five weeks: typical wait for an executor's appointment once the petition is in.
  • Four months: creditors have 4 months after actual notice to file claims.
  • Six months again: an estate with assets left after allowances and debts can't close earlier than 6 months after death.

The executor lists and safeguards assets, pays valid creditor claims (selling property if needed) and hands out the remainder. Acting on a dead person's property without appointment can make you personally liable. Wait to list, repair or remove anything until an attorney confirms who has authority.

Some assets pass outside the will: real estate in joint tenancy with right of survivorship, real estate titled in transfer on death form, life insurance, and pay on death accounts.

Transfer on death deeds are governed by K.S.A. 59-3501 and following. The owner names a beneficiary in a deed that must be executed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds where the land sits while the owner is alive (K.S.A. 59-3502). At the owner's death, title vests in the beneficiary (K.S.A. 59-3504). Recording in Johnson County runs $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page.

If there was no will and the estate is only real estate, a Determination of Descent can be started any time after 6 months from death. It usually wraps up in about 30 days.

sections.h2: Property tax while the estate is open
sections.html:
Probate doesn't pause the tax bills, and the county keeps mailing them. In Johnson County, the treasurer collects either in full by December 20 or in two halves, due December 20 and May 10, with interest on late payments under K.S.A. 79-2004. A bill you never received doesn't stop interest.

There, tax still unpaid by July 31 is published in the newspaper with a $15 fee, a lien attaches on the first Tuesday in September, and a foreclosure suit follows if the redemption period runs out. Procedures differ by county, so call the treasurer where the house stands. If the executor pays from estate funds, a future buyer gets clean title.

Paying taxes and debts on time is part of the executor's duty, so rank the tax bill above cosmetic repairs.

sections.h2: How an estate sale differs at closing
sections.html:
A sale out of an estate has a few extra stops that an ordinary listing lacks. The buyer's title company wants to see the document that gives the seller power to sign, whether that is court letters, a recorded beneficiary deed or a death certificate paired with a joint tenancy deed. Any lender with a mortgage on the house must be paid off from the proceeds, and the tax account must be current.

Where several heirs share the house, all of them, or the executor on their behalf, have to agree on price and terms. A single holdout can stall the deal for months. Talk through the plan as a family before a contract is signed, and write down who is responsible for utilities and insurance in the meantime.

After closing, the proceeds go to the estate or directly to the heirs, depending on the court's instructions. Keep the settlement statement, because it supports the sale price used when the gain is figured.

sections.h2: A practical order of steps for heirs
sections.html:
Work in this order: establish who has authority, check the tax account, and only then choose between holding and selling.

  • Learn how title is held: transfer on death deed, joint tenancy, or the probate estate.
  • Call the county treasurer about the tax account, because unpaid tax earns interest and can end in foreclosure.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing for your basis records.
  • Keep insurance active and the doors locked until the court process ends.
  • If probate applies, list only after the personal representative has written court authority.

Heirs who live far away, or who inherit a house that needs work, sometimes pick a direct as-is sale to stop paying taxes, utilities and upkeep while probate runs. The choice is yours, and the legal steps are the same either way. Cash buyers still ask for proof of authority, clear title and a paid-up tax account, so having those on hand shortens any closing. Bring the letters from the court, the deed, recent tax statements and the date-of-death value to your first meeting with a buyer or attorney.

faqs.q: Is there a Kansas inheritance tax on a house I inherit?
faqs.a: No Kansas death tax applies to anyone who died after December 31, 2009. The Department of Revenue won't process estate tax returns for those deaths.

faqs.q: What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?
faqs.a: For a 2026 death the federal basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000, and smaller estates generally owe nothing.

faqs.q: Do I need probate before selling an inherited Kansas house?
faqs.a: Often, when the house was in the decedent's name alone. Joint tenancy property and houses under a recorded transfer on death deed skip probate.

faqs.q: How long do I have to open probate in Kansas?
faqs.a: No later than 6 months after death. An executor is typically appointed 4 to 5 weeks after the petition is filed.

faqs.q: What is my tax basis in an inherited house?
faqs.a: Usually its market value when the owner died, unless you or your spouse gave it to the deceased within a year before death.
